content: The systematic review investigates the relationship between anthropometric measurements during infancy and childhood and the risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD) or type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in later life. 1. Cardiovascular Disease (CVD): Higher body mass index (BMI) during childhood was associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in adulthood in four cohort studies. The Helsinki Birth Cohort study found that lower BMI during early childhood was linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease in adulthood. Two cohort studies (one from the UK and one from the US) did not find any association between childhood BMI and adult CVD. Pooled results from three British cohorts showed that being persistently overweight from childhood to adulthood was significantly associated with coronary artery disease in later life. Historical British birth cohorts attributed minimal risk for ischemic heart disease to high childhood BMI. The Helsinki study also showed that lower weight and/or shorter height at one year of age increased morbidity and mortality due to coronary artery disease in adulthood. 2. Stroke: Four studies assessed the risk of developing atherosclerotic cerebrovascular events in relation to childhood BMI. One study found a positive association between lower childhood BMI and stroke-related mortality and morbidity in adulthood. Another study showed a positive relationship between childhood BMI and stroke risk in males only. Two studies did not find any association between childhood BMI and stroke in adulthood. The Helsinki cohort study indicated that lower weight at ages 1–7 years increased stroke-related morbidity and mortality in adulthood, but no association was found with childhood height. 3. Hypertension: Five articles (including three consortia) from 13 cohorts reported associations between anthropometric measures during infancy and childhood and the risk of developing hypertension in later life. A pooled analysis from five lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) showed that higher conditional weights (CW) were associated with increased blood pressure (BP) and odds of pre-hypertension or hypertension. However, when adjusted for adult height and BMI, CW during childhood was not associated with adult BP. Pooled analysis from three high-income countries (HICs) showed that individuals who were overweight or obese in childhood but non-obese as adults had similar hypertension risks to those with consistently normal BMI. Conversely, individuals who were obese as adults, regardless of childhood adiposity status, had increased hypertension risk. Nine studies observed positive associations between childhood/adolescence BMI and adult systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP), while two studies showed inverse or no associations. Six studies from four cohorts demonstrated a positive association between childhood/adolescence height and adult SBP. Three reports from different cohorts linked childhood/adolescence weight to adult DBP. No association was observed between infant length/weight and adolescent SBP in the Peruvian Birth Cohort. Two studies (NHLBI and ALSPAC) found that rapid increases in waist circumference were associated with higher odds of developing high SBP and DBP in adolescence. Two studies found a positive association between adolescent skinfold thickness and increased SBP and DBP in adulthood. One study reported a weak positive association between adolescent triceps skinfold thickness and adult DBP, and a strong positive correlation between subscapular skinfold thickness and adult DBP in females. 4. Carotid Intima-Media Thickness (cIMT): Fourteen reports (nine cohorts and one consortium) studied the relationship between childhood/adolescent BMI and cIMT levels in adulthood. Five studies showed a positive association between childhood/adolescent BMI and adult cIMT levels. One LMIC study found no association when adjusted for adult waist circumference. Two studies established that individuals who were obese in childhood and remained obese in adulthood had the highest cIMT levels, while those who normalized their weight in adulthood did not have elevated cIMT levels. One HIC study showed that shorter height at age 4 and less height gain between ages 2–4 were associated with higher cIMT levels in adulthood. However, an LMIC study found that taller height at age 2 and greater height gain from birth to age 2 were associated with higher cIMT levels, but this relationship was attenuated after adjusting for adult waist circumference. Two HIC studies showed that weight gain during infancy was associated with higher cIMT levels in adulthood. One study found a significant positive relationship between childhood triceps skinfold thickness and cIMT levels, while another study found this relationship to be positive only in girls. 5. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM): Ten articles from eight cohorts and three consortia discussed the associations between anthropometric measures during infancy/childhood and the development of T2DM in later life. Pooled analysis of three British birth cohorts (1946, 1958, and 1970) demonstrated that adult obesity combined with any pattern of earlier life overweight was associated with increased odds of T2DM. Another pooled analysis from three HIC cohorts reported that childhood overweight/obesity was a predictor of adult T2DM, except for one cohort that showed no association. In a pooled analysis from five LMICs, weight at 2 years, 4 years, and CW gain between birth and 4 years showed no association with impaired fasting glucose (IFG) or T2DM. However, when adjusted for adult waist circumference, these measures were inversely associated with IFG/T2DM. Two studies found that higher BMI (ages 4–18 years) was associated with increased risk of developing diabetes in adulthood. Two studies showed that individuals in the highest two quartiles during childhood had a high risk of mortality due to T2DM. Two other studies showed that lower weight at 1 or 2 years was associated with a higher risk of T2DM in adulthood. 6. HOMA-IR (Insulin Resistance): Six studies (four cohorts and one consortium) showed a relationship between childhood anthropometry and HOMA-IR levels in adulthood. In a pooled analysis from five LMICs, weight at 2 years, 4 years, and CW gain between birth and 4 years were significantly associated with HOMA-IR, but the association became inverse and non-significant after adjusting for adult waist circumference. One HIC cohort showed a positive association of HOMA-IR with childhood BMI, while another LMIC cohort showed that an increase in BMI between 6 months to 11 years was positively associated with HOMA-IR at 11 years. Two other HIC cohorts showed no association or an inverse association with HOMA-IR in later life. 7. Fasting Glucose Levels: Four studies reported positive associations between childhood BMI and fasting glucose levels in adulthood. One study showed no association between childhood BMI and fasting glucose levels in adulthood, while another study demonstrated no association between BMI during infancy and fasting glucose levels in childhood. Another study found that childhood BMI was inversely related to 2-hour glucose levels in adulthood. In a pooled analysis from five LMICs, weight at 2 years, 4 years, and CW gain between birth and 4 years showed no association with fasting glucose. However, when adjusted for adult waist circumference, these measures were inversely associated with fasting glucose. 8. Insulin Levels: Three HIC studies attributed positive associations of insulin levels in adulthood to childhood BMI levels. However, one study found the association to be inverse after adjusting for adult BMI. One study showed that a rapid increase in BMI during childhood increased the risk of high insulin levels in adolescence. Another study found that an increase in BMI between 6 months to 11 years was positively associated with higher fasting insulin levels at 11 years and adolescence. One study demonstrated a significant positive association between childhood weight, rate of increase in weight and height during childhood/adolescence, and adulthood insulin levels, but not with the rate of height increase during childhood/adolescence. Rapid increases in waist circumference were associated with higher odds of developing high insulin levels later in adolescence. Childhood triceps skinfold thickness positively correlated with adulthood insulin levels. 9. Overweight and Obesity: Fifty-two studies (36 cohort or longitudinal studies) provided information on the association of anthropometric measures during infancy and childhood with the risk of developing obesity in later life (childhood, adolescence, and adulthood). Meta-analysis using a random-effects model showed a significant inverse association of correlation coefficients between early-life anthropometric measures and later-life obesity risk. This detailed summary provides a comprehensive understanding of the associations between early-life anthropometric measures and long-term health outcomes.
